1.note: Jeremiah is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **exile**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 4, 16, 20, and 31. Alternate translation: [the people who had been taken away]

2.q: אַחֲרֵ֣י צֵ֣את יְכָנְיָֽה־הַ֠⁠מֶּלֶךְ וְ⁠הַ⁠גְּבִירָ֨ה וְ⁠הַ⁠סָּרִיסִ֜ים שָׂרֵ֨י יְהוּדָ֧ה וִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וְ⁠הֶ⁠חָרָ֥שׁ וְ⁠הַ⁠מַּסְגֵּ֖ר מִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
2.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the going out**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [after Jeconiah the king, and the queen mother, and the eunuchs, the princes of Judah and Jerusalem, and the craftsmen and the smiths, went out from Jerusalem]

2.q: אַחֲרֵ֣י צֵ֣את יְכָנְיָֽה־הַ֠⁠מֶּלֶךְ וְ⁠הַ⁠גְּבִירָ֨ה וְ⁠הַ⁠סָּרִיסִ֜ים שָׂרֵ֨י יְהוּדָ֧ה וִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִַ֛ם וְ⁠הֶ⁠חָרָ֥שׁ וְ⁠הַ⁠מַּסְגֵּ֖ר מִ⁠ירוּשָׁלִָֽם
2.note: Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Jeremiah is using the phrase **the princes of Judah and Jerusalem** to introduce a group of new participants in the story. If your language has its own way of introducing new participants, you could use it here in your translation. Alternate translation: [the leading officials of Judah and Jerusalem]

3.note: Here, **the hand** represents the action of a person who carries a message for someone else. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [He sent it by means of Elasah] or [He sent it with Elasah]

The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly. This also occurs in verses 22 and 30.

4.q: כֹּ֥ה אָמַ֛ר יְהוָ֥ה צְבָא֖וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֑ל
4.note: The phrase **Thus says Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel** introduces a direct quotation of what Yahweh says. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. This also occurs in verses 8, 10, 16, 21, 25, and 32 in this chapter.
See how you translated this name in 20:12.

In this verse, the word **exile** is singular in form, but it refers to all the exiled people as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “exile.” Alternate translation: [to all the exiles]

5.q: בְּנ֥וּ בָתִּ֖ים וְ⁠שֵׁ֑בוּ וְ⁠נִטְע֣וּ גַנּ֔וֹת וְ⁠אִכְל֖וּ אֶת־פִּרְיָֽ⁠ן
5.note: The implication is that Yahweh wants the exiles to settle in Babylon for a long time, rather than expecting to return to Judah soon. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [Build houses and settle down and live in them, since you will be there a long time, and plant gardens and eat their fruit]

6.q: וְ⁠אֶת־בְּנֽוֹתֵי⁠כֶם֙ תְּנ֣וּ לַֽ⁠אֲנָשִׁ֔ים וְ⁠תֵלַ֖דְנָה בָּנִ֣ים וּ⁠בָנ֑וֹת
6.note: Here, **that** marks **they may bear sons and daughters** as the goal or purpose of **give your daughters to men**. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [let your daughters marry for the purpose of producing new families]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **few**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [and keep increasing in number there]

7.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how the city may be at peace]

It might seem that the expression **where I have exiled you there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where I have exiled you]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [because when that city has peace, there shall be peace for you]

8.q: כִּי֩ כֹ֨ה אָמַ֜ר יְהוָ֤ה צְבָאוֹת֙ אֱלֹהֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֔ל
8.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 29:4.

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **deceive**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [Let your prophets who are in your midst and your diviners tell you the truth]

9.note: If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **falsehood**, you could express the same idea in another way. This also occurs in verses 21 and 31. Alternate translation: [in deception]

Yahweh is using the term **name** to represent his own authority. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. This also occurs in verses 21, 23, and 25. Alternate translation: [as if I had authorized them]
See how you translated **the declaration of Yahweh** in 1:8. This also occurs in verses 11, 14, 19, 23, and 32.

10.q: כִּ֠י לְ⁠פִ֞י מְלֹ֧את לְ⁠בָבֶ֛ל שִׁבְעִ֥ים שָׁנָ֖ה
10.note: The expression **is completed** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. If you need to say who does the action, the context indicates that it is Yahweh. Alternate translation: [When I complete seventy years for Babylon]

Yahweh is using **I will visit you** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will come to help you.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will attend to you and help you]

Yahweh is using the term **word** to represent what he promised by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [the good thing that I promised]

11.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **I myself** separately, even though the verb translated as **know** already includes this meaning. He is doing that to emphasize that he alone is aware of what he intends to do for the exiles. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing the meaning here. Alternate translation: [For I alone know the plans]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **plans**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [what I am planning]
This is poetic language. If your language has a way to indicate poetry, you could use it here. Alternate translation: [the thoughts that I am thinking]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **peace**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [plans to make you prosper]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **evil**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [harming you]

The phrase **a future and a hope** expresses a single idea. The word **hope** tells more about **a future**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [a future full of hope]

12.note: The phrase **call to me and pray to me** expresses a single idea. The word **pray** tells more about **call**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [pray earnestly to me]

13.note: Here, **your heart** represents where your thoughts and desires exist. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [with all your thoughts and desires]

14.note: The expression **I will be found** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And you will find me]

Jeremiah is using a construction in which a verb and its object come from the same root. You may be able to use the same construction in your language to express the meaning here. Alternatively, your language may have another way of saying this as in the UST.
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **restoration**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [and I will cause them to prosper again]

It might seem that the expression **where I have driven you there** contains extra information that would not be natural to express in your language. If so, you could shorten it. Alternate translation: [where I have scattered you]

This could mean: (1) that Yahweh would cause the people of Judah to prosper again. Alternate translation: [and I will cause you to prosper again] or [and I will restore your fortunes] (2) that Yahweh would cause them to return from their captivity. Alternate translation: [and I will cause you to return from your captivity]

15.note: The word translated as **Because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what comes after it. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what comes after it. Alternate translation: [Since you have said]

16.note: Jeremiah is providing background information to help readers understand what happens next in the story. In your translation, introduce this information in a way that would be natural in your own language and culture.

Here, **the throne of David** represents the royal authority that David once had. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [ruling with the royal authority that David once had]

Jeremiah is not referring to a specific **people**. He means people in general, that is, the residents of Jerusalem as a group. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use an expression that would be more natural in your language. Alternate translation: [and about the residents of this city]

The pronoun **you** refers to the people whom Yahweh had sent into exile in Babylon. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [your brothers who did not go out with you exiles into the exile]
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:19.

17.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me sending** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to send]
See how you translated the similar expression in 24:10.

The point of this comparison is that just as **the horrible figs that cannot be eaten** are worthless and repulsive to anyone who sees them, so the people who remained in Jerusalem will become worthless and repulsive. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [as worthless and repulsive as horrible figs that no one can eat]

The expression **cannot be eaten** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [that no one can eat because they are so bad]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **badness**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how rotten they are]

18.note: See how you translated this expression in 14:12. This also occurs in verse 17.

18.q: ל⁠זועה לְ⁠כֹ֣ל מַמְלְכ֣וֹת הָ⁠אָ֗רֶץ לְ⁠אָלָ֤ה וּ⁠לְ⁠שַׁמָּה֙ וְ⁠לִ⁠שְׁרֵקָ֣ה וּ⁠לְ⁠חֶרְפָּ֔ה
18.note: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **a horror**, **a curse**, **a desolation**, **a hissing**, and **a reproach**, you could express the same ideas in another way. Alternate translation: [something horrifying to all the kingdoms of the earth, a people whom others curse and a people who appall others and a people whom others hiss at and a people whom others scorn]
See how you translated the similar expression in 24:9.

Hissing at someone was a symbolic action by which people of this culture showed their contempt and horror at what had happened to that person. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text of your translation or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [a cause for people to hiss in contempt]
See how you translated the similar expression in 19:8.

19.note: The word translated as **because** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [since]
Yahweh is using the term **words** to represent what he said by using words. If it would be clearer in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [my messages]

The implication is that these prophets spoke to the people on Yahweh’s behalf and with his authority. You could include this information if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [by my servants the prophets, who spoke with my authority]

Yahweh is speaking as if the prophets were his **servants**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [by the prophets who serve me]
See how you translated **rising early and sending** in 25:4.

The pronoun **you** refers to the people who were already in exile in Babylon, while the pronoun **them** refers to the people who remained in Jerusalem. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [but you exiles did not listen either]

20.note: Yahweh is stating the pronoun **you** separately, even though the verb translated as **hear** already includes this meaning. He is doing that because he is contrasting the exiles in Babylon with the people who remained in Jerusalem. If a speaker of your language would use an explicit pronoun for the same purpose, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of showing that meaning here. Alternate translation: [But as for you, be sure you hear the word of Yahweh]
See how you translated the similar expression in 8:9. This also occurs in verse 30.

In this verse, the word **exile** is singular in form, but it refers to all the exiles as a group. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use the plural form of “exile.” Alternate translation: [all you exiles]

21.note: Yahweh is using **Behold me** as a common expression of the culture to mean that he was about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to give]

Jeremiah is using **Thus says Yahweh of Armies** to introduce a direct quotation from Yahweh. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. See how you translated this phrase in verse 29:4.

Here, **the hand** represents the power of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [into the power of Nebuchadnezzar]
Yahweh is using the term **eyes** to mean sight. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [while you watch]

22.q: וְ⁠לֻקַּ֤ח מֵ⁠הֶם֙ קְלָלָ֔ה לְ⁠כֹל֙ גָּל֣וּת יְהוּדָ֔ה אֲשֶׁ֥ר בְּ⁠בָבֶ֖ל לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר
22.note: The expression **a curse shall be taken up** is a passive verbal form. If it would be unnatural to use that form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [And because of them, all the exile of Judah who are in Babylon shall take up a curse, saying]

Yahweh is using **a curse shall be taken up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “people will speak a curse.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [a curse shall come into use]
See how you translated this phrase in verse 29:4.

22.q: יְשִֽׂמְ⁠ךָ֤ יְהוָה֙ כְּ⁠צִדְקִיָּ֣הוּ וּ⁠כְ⁠אֶחָ֔ב אֲשֶׁר־קָלָ֥⁠ם מֶֽלֶךְ־בָּבֶ֖ל בָּ⁠אֵֽשׁ
22.note: This is the beginning of what the exiles of Judah will say when they curse someone. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a third-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a third-level quotation.

The point of this comparison is that just as **Zedekiah** and **Ahab** died a terrible death, so the person being cursed would die a terrible death. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [die a terrible death like Zedekiah and Ahab]

23.note: Yahweh is using **they have done a shameful thing in Israel** as a common expression of the culture to mean “they have committed an outrageous sin among the people of Israel.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [they have committed an outrageous sin among the people of Israel]

24.note: The word **Shemaiah** is the name of a man.
The word **Nehelamite** is the name of a people group.

25.q: כֹּֽה־אָמַ֞ר יְהוָ֧ה צְבָא֛וֹת אֱלֹהֵ֥י יִשְׂרָאֵ֖ל לֵ⁠אמֹ֑ר
25.note: The phrase **Thus says Yahweh of hosts, the God of Israel, saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent the term **saying** explicitly.

This is the beginning of what Yahweh said to Shemaiah. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a second-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a second-level quotation.

26.note: This is the beginning of what Shemaiah wrote in the letters that he sent. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a third-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a third-level quotation.
See how you translated the similar expression in 17:26.

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [every person who is raving]

Zephaniah is using **making himself a prophet** as a common expression of the culture to mean that a person claims to have the ability and authority to speak messages from God, when he does not actually have that ability and authority. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and setting himself up as a prophet] or [and claiming that he is a prophet]

A **neck iron** is a kind of metal collar that was fastened around a prisoner’s neck to hold him in place. If your readers would not be familiar with what a neck iron is, you could use the name of a similar thing that your readers would recognize, or you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [the metal collar]

27.q: לָ֚⁠מָּה לֹ֣א גָעַ֔רְתָּ בְּ⁠יִרְמְיָ֖הוּ הָֽ⁠עֲנְּתֹתִ֑י הַ⁠מִּתְנַבֵּ֖א לָ⁠כֶֽם
27.note: Shemaiah is using the question form to rebuke Zephaniah for not stopping Jeremiah from speaking. If a speaker of your language would not use the question form for that purpose, you could translate this as a statement or as an exclamation. Alternate translation: [you should have rebuked Jeremiah, the Anathothite, the one making himself a prophet to you.]
The pronoun **you** refers to Zephaniah the priest. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [why have you, Zephaniah, not rebuked Jeremiah the Anathothite]

This is a double negative, consisting of the negative particle **not** and the negative word **rebuked**. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use a positive expression to translate this. Alternate translation: [why have you allowed]

28.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [The reason I say this is that he has sent to us in Babylon]

28.q: אֲרֻכָּ֣ה הִ֑יא בְּנ֤וּ בָתִּים֙ וְ⁠שֵׁ֔בוּ וְ⁠נִטְע֣וּ גַנּ֔וֹת וְ⁠אִכְל֖וּ אֶת־פְּרִי⁠הֶֽן
28.note: This is the beginning of what Shemaiah says that Jeremiah wrote. You may wish to mark the words of this speech with a fourth-level quotation mark at the beginning and end of them or with some other punctuation or convention that your language uses to indicate a fourth-level quotation.

29.note: Jeremiah is using the word translated as **And** to introduce a new event in the story. Use a word, phrase, or other method in your language that is natural for introducing a new event.
Jeremiah is using the term **ears** to mean hearing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [aloud to Jeremiah]

30.note: See how you translated the similar expression in 1:4.

31.note: The term **saying** introduces a direct quotation. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language. It may not be necessary to represent this term explicitly.
The phrase **Thus says Yahweh** introduces a direct quotation of what Yahweh says. In your translation, use a natural way of introducing direct quotations in your language.
See how you translated the similar expression in 28:15.

32.note: The term translated as **therefore** indicates that what follows is a result of what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [as a result, this is what Yahweh says]

Yahweh is using **Behold me** as an expression that people of this culture would commonly use to mean that they were about to do something. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [Now I am about to bring punishment]

Yahweh is using **visiting punishment upon** as a common expression of the culture to mean “punishing.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [bringing down punishment on] or [punishing]
See how you translated “seed” in 7:15 where it is used with the same meaning. Alternate translation: [the people descended from him]

Here the masculine term **man** has a generic sense that includes both men and women. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could use language in your translation that is clearly inclusive of both men and women. Alternate translation: [anyone dwelling]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **the good**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [how kindly I am acting]

Here, **rebellion** represents words that urge people to rebel. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [he has spoken words urging people to rebel against Yahweh]
